lessons.title: Getting to Know Spanish Letters
lessons.summary: Spanish has 27 letters, including ñ.

examples.explanation: España contains ñ, a distinct letter pronounced roughly like 'ny' in canyon. Bonita describes España and takes feminine agreement.
Niño contains ñ, a separate Spanish letter. El agrees with the masculine singular noun niño.

lessons.title: The Five Vowel Sounds
lessons.summary: Spanish vowels generally have consistent sounds.
keywords: spanish vowels generally have consistent sounds.

examples.explanation: Casa has two clear a vowels. Pequeña contains the letter ñ; its final -a agrees with the feminine noun casa.

examples.english: The moon lights up the patio.
examples.explanation: The vowels in luna and patio retain their characteristic sounds; Spanish vowels are usually not reduced to a neutral schwa.

lessons.title: Know Where the Stress Goes
lessons.summary: Find a word’s prominent syllable with spelling and accent rules.
keywords: every spanish word has a stressed syllable.

examples.explanation: Papá has an accent because the final syllable is stressed, unlike the usual pattern for a word ending in a vowel.
Teléfono is stressed on lé; the written accent marks stress outside the default penultimate-syllable pattern.

lessons.title: The Two R Sounds
lessons.summary: A single r and rr can sound different.
keywords: a single r and rr can sound different.

examples.explanation: Perro and corre contain rr, pronounced with a trill. Compare pero, which has a single tapped r.

examples.english: I want to, but I cannot.
examples.explanation: Quiero and pero use a single tapped r between vowels, unlike the trilled rr in perro.

lessons.title: Why Words Use El or La
lessons.summary: Nouns have grammatical gender.
lessons.grammarTerm: Why Words Use El or La
keywords: why words use el or la

examples.explanation: Libro is masculine and uses el. Nuevo changes to its masculine singular form to describe libro.
Puerta is feminine, so it takes la and the feminine adjective abierta.

lessons.title: When to Use El, La, Un, and Una
lessons.summary: Articles show whether a thing is identifiable or newly introduced.
lessons.grammarTerm: When to Use El, La, Un, and Una
keywords: when to use el, la, un, and una
articles show whether a thing is identifiable or newly introduced.

examples.explanation: Un is a masculine singular indefinite article. It introduces a book without identifying which one.
La identifies a particular girl; una introduces a nonspecific feminine singular backpack.

lessons.title: Talking About More Than One
lessons.summary: Nouns and related words change for number.
keywords: nouns and related words change for number.

examples.explanation: La becomes las, casa becomes casas, and grande becomes grandes. All three agree in plural number.
Árbol becomes árboles, el becomes los, and alto becomes altos to agree with the plural subject.

lessons.title: Describing People and Things
lessons.summary: Describing words often agree with nouns.
keywords: describing words often agree with nouns.

examples.explanation: Roja follows mesa and ends in -a to match the feminine singular noun.
Negros and nuevos both agree with zapatos in masculine plural; descriptive adjectives commonly follow the noun.

lessons.title: Saying More, Less, and As Much
lessons.summary: Compare qualities using más, menos and tan.
lessons.grammarTerm: Saying More, Less, and As Much
keywords: saying more, less, and as much
compare qualities using más, menos and tan.

examples.spanish: Ana es más alta que Luis.
examples.explanation: Más ... que expresses a comparison. Alta agrees with Ana, the person being described.

examples.spanish: Este café es tan bueno como aquel.
examples.english: This coffee is as good as that one.
examples.explanation: Tan + adjective + como expresses equality, rather than the más ... que pattern for superiority.

lessons.title: Saying I, You, and We
lessons.summary: Verb endings often identify who acts.
keywords: verb endings often identify who acts.

examples.explanation: Compro comes from comprar: remove -ar and add -o for first-person singular. Yo (I) is implied by the verb ending.
Vivimos is the nosotros form of vivir. The subject pronoun nosotros can be omitted because -imos signals first-person plural.
Trabajas is the tú form of trabajar. The subject tú is omitted because -as identifies the person addressed.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Say You
lessons.summary: Tú and usted have different verb patterns.
keywords: tú and usted have different verb patterns.

examples.explanation: Usted addresses one person formally, but takes the third-person singular form habla, not hablas.
Tú uses the second-person singular ending -as in estudias, unlike usted estudia.

lessons.title: Saying My, Your, and Their
lessons.summary: Possessive words show who something belongs to.
keywords: possessive words show who something belongs to.

examples.explanation: Sus is plural because libros is plural. The form does not tell you whether the owner is one person or several.

examples.english: My sister is looking for our keys.
examples.explanation: Mi does not change for gender; nuestras agrees in feminine plural with llaves, not with the owners.

lessons.title: Replacing Things with Lo and La
lessons.summary: Short words replace objects in a sentence.
lessons.grammarTerm: Replacing Things with Lo and La
keywords: replacing things with lo and la
short words replace objects in a sentence.

examples.english: I have the book. I read it.
examples.explanation: Lo replaces el libro, a masculine singular direct object. It appears before the conjugated verb leo.

examples.english: Do you see María? Yes, I see her.
examples.explanation: La replaces the feminine singular direct object María and comes before the conjugated verb veo.

lessons.title: Actions You Do to Yourself
lessons.summary: Some verbs use a pronoun referring back to the subject.
keywords: some verbs use a pronoun referring back to the subject.

examples.explanation: Se refers to ella. Spanish normally uses las manos instead of a possessive such as her hands here.
Despertarse is reflexive here: me refers back to the speaker, and despierto is the yo present-tense form.

lessons.title: What Is a Verb's Base Form?
lessons.summary: Dictionary-form verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir.
lessons.grammarTerm: What Is a Verb's Base Form?
keywords: what is a verb's base form?

examples.explanation: Comer is an infinitive ending in -er. Quiero is the first-person singular form of querer.
Salir stays in its infinitive form after the conjugated verb necesitamos; only the first verb carries person and tense.

lessons.title: Talking About What You Do
lessons.summary: Regular -ar verbs change endings by subject.
keywords: regular -ar verbs change endings by subject.

examples.explanation: Compra comes from comprar: remove -ar and add -a for third-person singular. Ella makes the subject explicit.
Hablamos comes from hablar: remove -ar and add -amos for first-person plural in the present tense.

lessons.title: More Ways Verbs Change
lessons.summary: Regular -er and -ir verbs share some endings.
keywords: regular -er and -ir verbs share some endings.

examples.explanation: Vive comes from vivir: remove -ir and add -e for third-person singular.
Comes is the tú present-tense form of comer, formed with the -es ending for regular -er verbs.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Say To Be
lessons.summary: Ser identifies or characterizes; estar often describes states and locations.
lessons.grammarTerm: Two Ways to Say To Be
keywords: two ways to say to be
ser identifies or characterizes; estar often describes states and locations.

examples.explanation: Estoy is first-person singular of estar. Cansada describes the speaker's state and uses feminine agreement.
Ser expresses identity or profession. Compare está cansada, where estar describes a current condition.
Estar describes the soup's current state or temperature; es fría would characterize it as habitually cold.

lessons.title: Saying There Is or There Are
lessons.summary: Hay introduces the existence of things.
lessons.grammarTerm: Saying There Is or There Are
keywords: saying there is or there are
hay introduces the existence of things.

examples.explanation: Hay stays the same even though ventanas is plural. Tres tells us there are three windows.

examples.spanish: No hay leche en la nevera.
examples.english: There is no milk in the refrigerator.
examples.explanation: Hay is the impersonal form meaning there is or there are; it does not change for singular or plural nouns.

lessons.title: Talking About What You're Going to Do
lessons.summary: Use ir + a + infinitive for plans.
lessons.grammarTerm: Talking About What You're Going to Do
keywords: talking about what you're going to do
use ir + a + infinitive for plans.

examples.explanation: Voy is first-person singular of ir. A connects it to the infinitive estudiar, which does not change.

examples.spanish: Vamos a visitar a mis abuelos.
examples.english: We are going to visit my grandparents.
examples.explanation: Vamos a + infinitive visitar expresses a planned or near-future action; the personal a marks the people visited.

lessons.title: Talking About Completed Past Actions
lessons.summary: The preterite presents past events as completed.
keywords: the preterite presents past events as completed.

examples.explanation: Compré comes from comprar. The accented -é ending signals first-person singular preterite, unlike present compro.

examples.english: Last night we ate dinner together.
examples.explanation: Cenamos is a regular -ar preterite nosotros form; anoche places the completed event in the past.

examples.english: On Saturday we went to the museum.
examples.explanation: Fuimos is the irregular preterite nosotros form of ir (also of ser); al museo and the context indicate movement.

lessons.title: Describing How Things Used to Be
lessons.summary: The imperfect often describes past habits or background.
lessons.grammarTerm: Describing How Things Used to Be
keywords: describing how things used to be
the imperfect often describes past habits or background.

examples.explanation: Vivíamos comes from vivir and uses -íamos for first-person plural imperfect. Antes places the habit in an earlier period.

examples.spanish: De niño, jugaba en el parque.
examples.english: As a child, I used to play in the park.
examples.explanation: Jugaba is the imperfect of jugar and describes a repeated habit in the past, not one bounded event.

lessons.title: An Event Versus the Background
lessons.summary: Contrast bounded past events with ongoing context.
keywords: contrast bounded past events with ongoing context.

examples.english: I was reading when the phone rang.
examples.explanation: Leía is imperfect because reading was ongoing. Sonó is preterite because the ringing is presented as an event.

examples.english: While I was cooking, Ana arrived.
examples.explanation: Cocinaba is imperfect background action; llegó is preterite for the completed event that happened during it.

lessons.title: Talking About What Will Happen
lessons.summary: Future endings attach to the infinitive.
keywords: future endings attach to the infinitive.

examples.explanation: Estudiaré combines estudiar with the first-person future ending -é. The accent marks the stressed ending.

examples.english: Next year we will learn more.
examples.explanation: Aprenderemos adds -emos to the full infinitive aprender to form the nosotros simple future.

lessons.title: Talking About What Would Happen
lessons.summary: Conditional forms describe imagined outcomes and polite requests.
keywords: conditional forms describe imagined outcomes and polite requests.

examples.explanation: Podrías is the tú conditional form of poder. The conditional makes this request softer than a direct command.
Gustaría is the conditional of gustar, used here to make a polite request.

lessons.title: Expressing Wishes and Uncertainty
lessons.summary: Some expressions require a subjunctive verb.
keywords: some expressions require a subjunctive verb.

examples.explanation: Espero que expresses a hope. Tengas is the tú present subjunctive of tener, rather than indicative tienes.

examples.english: It is important that you rest.
examples.explanation: The expression es importante que introduces a judgment; descanses is present subjunctive after que.

lessons.title: Putting a Simple Sentence Together
lessons.summary: Spanish often uses subject–verb–object order.

examples.explanation: Ana is the subject, lee is the conjugated form of leer, and un libro is what she reads.
The time expression ayer can lead the sentence while the subject María still precedes the verb compró.

lessons.title: Asking Questions
lessons.summary: Spanish marks questions at both ends.
keywords: spanish marks questions at both ends.

examples.explanation: Dónde carries a written accent as a question word. Vives is the tú form of vivir; the subject tú is implied.
Cuándo takes a written accent in a direct question, and Spanish questions use opening and closing question marks.

lessons.title: Saying No and Not
lessons.summary: No usually comes before a conjugated verb.
keywords: no usually comes before a conjugated verb.

examples.explanation: No comes before tengo to negate the statement. Tengo is the first-person singular of tener.
Nunca before the verb already negates the sentence; no is not needed before como.

lessons.title: Connecting Two Ideas
lessons.summary: Words such as porque and pero join ideas.
keywords: words such as porque and pero join ideas.

examples.english: I study because I want to learn.
examples.explanation: Porque introduces the reason. Quiero is the first-person singular of querer and is followed by the infinitive aprender.

examples.english: I wanted to go out, but it was raining.
examples.explanation: Pero introduces contrast between the wish to leave and the reason that prevented it.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Say For
lessons.summary: Por and para express different relationships.
keywords: por and para express different relationships.

examples.english: I study in order to learn.
examples.explanation: Para introduces the purpose of studying and is followed by the infinitive aprender.
Por introduces the reason for the thanks; para instead commonly expresses purpose or destination.

lessons.title: Saying What You Like
lessons.summary: Gustar agrees with the thing liked.
keywords: gustar agrees with the thing liked.

examples.explanation: Gustan is plural because los libros is plural. Me identifies the person experiencing the liking.

examples.spanish: A mi hermano le gusta bailar.
examples.explanation: Le marks the person who experiences the liking; gusta is singular because the infinitive bailar is what pleases him.

lessons.title: Giving Instructions and Requests
lessons.summary: Commands have special affirmative and negative forms.
keywords: commands have special affirmative and negative forms.

examples.explanation: Negative tú commands use the present subjunctive hables, not the affirmative command habla.
Escucha is an affirmative tú command of escuchar; affirmative regular -ar tú commands use the él/ella present form.

lessons.title: Read the Accent Mark
lessons.summary: Understand written accents, tilde rules and meaning contrasts.
lessons.grammarTerm: When Words Need an Accent Mark
keywords: when words need an accent mark
accent marks indicate stress or distinguish words.

examples.explanation: Tú with an accent means you; tu without an accent means your. Tienes is the tú form of tener.
Él with an accent is the subject pronoun he; el without an accent is the definite article the.

lessons.title: Spanish Question and Exclamation Marks
lessons.summary: Direct questions and exclamations have opening marks.
keywords: direct questions and exclamations have opening marks.

examples.explanation: The inverted exclamation mark starts the exclamation. Qué has a written accent in this exclamatory use.
Spanish opens questions with ¿ and exclamations with ¡, then closes each with its matching mark.

lessons.title: What Does Se Mean Here?
lessons.summary: Se appears in several grammatical patterns.
keywords: se appears in several grammatical patterns.

examples.explanation: Se venden is a passive se construction. Venden agrees with the plural noun libros.
Se + third-person singular habla expresses an impersonal statement without naming who speaks.

lessons.title: Imagining Different Outcomes
lessons.summary: Hypothetical conditions often combine subjunctive and conditional.
keywords: hypothetical conditions often combine subjunctive and conditional.

examples.english: If I had time, I would travel.
examples.explanation: Tuviera is imperfect subjunctive of tener after si; viajaría is conditional and expresses the imagined result.

examples.spanish: Si ganara la lotería, compraría una casa.
examples.english: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
examples.explanation: Si + imperfect subjunctive ganara sets an unreal condition; compraría is conditional for the imagined result.

lessons.title: Read Spanish Letter Combinations
lessons.summary: Read ll, ch, qu and other spellings as sound patterns.
keywords: Read ll, ch, qu and other spellings as sound patterns.

examples.explanation: Ll in llave is one consonant spelling; do not pronounce two l sounds.
Ch works together; qu before i/e preserves a k sound with silent u.

lessons.title: Find the Beat in a Word
lessons.summary: Separate syllables before finding the stressed one.
lessons.grammarTerm: Find the Beat in a Word
keywords: Separate syllables before finding the stressed one.

examples.explanation: Casa divides ca-sa and normally stresses ca.
Teléfono divides te-lé-fo-no; the written accent identifies lé.

lessons.title: When Vowels Meet
lessons.summary: Learn when adjacent vowels share a syllable or separate.
keywords: Learn when adjacent vowels share a syllable or separate.

examples.explanation: Río has two syllables, rí-o. The accent marks a stressed i separated from o.
The ie in tiempo shares a syllable: tiem-po.

lessons.title: Put the Focus Where You Mean It
lessons.summary: Emphasize a word without changing its normal stressed syllable.
lessons.grammarTerm: Put the Focus Where You Mean It
keywords: Emphasize a word without changing its normal stressed syllable.

examples.spanish: Yo tengo la llave, no Ana.
examples.english: I have the key, not Ana.
examples.explanation: The explicit pronoun supports a contrast about who has the key.

examples.spanish: Tengo la llave, no el mapa.
examples.english: I have the key, not the map.
examples.explanation: The contrast concerns the object, not the subject.

lessons.title: Find Your Way Through a Sentence
lessons.summary: Use prepositions to locate things and describe movement.
lessons.grammarTerm: Find Your Way Through a Sentence
keywords: Use prepositions to locate things and describe movement.

examples.spanish: La caja está debajo del mapa.
examples.english: The box is under the map.
examples.explanation: Debajo de is one location pattern; de + el contracts to del.

examples.english: They walk as far as a bridge.
examples.explanation: Hasta marks the endpoint of the walk.

lessons.title: Place Events in Time
lessons.summary: Read clock times, parts of the day and before/after relationships.
keywords: Read clock times, parts of the day and before/after relationships.

examples.spanish: El tren sale a las ocho.
examples.explanation: A las places the departure at a clock time.
The plural article expresses a repeated weekday.

lessons.title: Who Receives It?
lessons.summary: Distinguish the thing given from the person receiving it.
keywords: Distinguish the thing given from the person receiving it.

examples.explanation: Le marks the recipient; agua is the offered thing.

examples.spanish: Les doy las llaves a mis amigas.
examples.english: I give the keys to my friends.
examples.explanation: Les agrees in number with the recipients, not with llaves.

lessons.title: Put the Pronouns Together
lessons.summary: Combine recipient and object pronouns in a predictable order.
keywords: Combine recipient and object pronouns in a predictable order.

examples.explanation: Se replaces le before lo; a Ana clarifies the recipient.

examples.english: He/she brings them to me today.
examples.explanation: Me comes before las, which replaces a feminine plural object.

lessons.title: Recognize Verbs That Change Inside
lessons.summary: Read common stem changes and irregular present-tense forms.
keywords: Read common stem changes and irregular present-tense forms.

examples.explanation: Quiere comes from querer: the stem e changes to ie.
Tiene comes from tener and differs from the regular pattern.

lessons.title: Recognize Unexpected Past Forms
lessons.summary: Connect dijo, tuvo and other past forms to their infinitives.
keywords: Connect dijo, tuvo and other past forms to their infinitives.

examples.explanation: Dijo is the third-person preterite of decir.
Tuvieron comes from tener; the infinitive construction adds obligation.

lessons.title: Point to This, That, and the Other One
lessons.summary: Track what este, ese and aquel refer to.
lessons.grammarTerm: Point to This, That, and the Other One
keywords: Track what este, ese and aquel refer to.

examples.english: This morning he/she finds a key.
examples.explanation: Esta agrees with mañana and points to the current morning.

examples.english: He/she does not recognize that number.
examples.explanation: Ese identifies the number being discussed.

lessons.title: Describe the Person or Thing You Mean
lessons.summary: Use que and donde to attach a description to a noun.
lessons.grammarTerm: Describe the Person or Thing You Mean
keywords: Use que and donde to attach a description to a noun.

examples.spanish: Encontraron a una niña que sostenía una vela.
examples.english: They found a girl who was holding a candle.
examples.explanation: Que attaches sostenía una vela to niña.

examples.english: I am reading the book that you bought.
examples.explanation: You bought the book; the subject inside the relative clause differs from the main subject.

lessons.title: Read What Someone Says or Thinks
lessons.summary: Recognize que clauses that carry the content of a statement.
lessons.grammarTerm: Read What Someone Says or Thinks
keywords: Recognize que clauses that carry the content of a statement.

examples.spanish: Él dice que espera a alguien.
examples.english: He says that he is waiting for someone.
examples.explanation: Que introduces the content of dice.

examples.spanish: Ana cree que Luis tiene la llave.
examples.english: Ana thinks that Luis has the key.
examples.explanation: Each clause has its own subject and verb.

lessons.title: Recognize Actions Turned into Forms
lessons.summary: Distinguish verb compounds from descriptions such as escrita and cerrada.
keywords: Distinguish verb compounds from descriptions such as escrita and cerrada.

examples.explanation: After haber, escrito stays fixed even with feminine nota.

examples.spanish: La nota estaba escrita a mano.
examples.explanation: Escrita describes nota and agrees with it.

lessons.title: Connect a Past Event to Now
lessons.summary: Build he leído and understand its reference to the present.
lessons.grammarTerm: Connect a Past Event to Now
keywords: Build he leído and understand its reference to the present.

examples.explanation: He identifies yo; leído is the participle of leer.

examples.english: We have never seen that hotel.
examples.explanation: The experience is considered up to the present.

lessons.title: Go Back Before the Story’s Past
lessons.summary: Use había + participle for an event before another past moment.
lessons.grammarTerm: Go Back Before the Story’s Past
keywords: Use había + participle for an event before another past moment.

examples.spanish: Cuando llegué, Ana ya había salido.
examples.english: When I arrived, Ana had already left.
examples.explanation: Leaving precedes the arrival.

examples.english: His/her father had been a photographer.
examples.explanation: Había sido introduces an earlier layer of the father’s life.

lessons.title: Watch an Action Unfold
lessons.summary: Read estar + gerund and distinguish an action in progress from a habit.
keywords: Read estar + gerund and distinguish an action in progress from a habit.

examples.explanation: Estaba sets the past reference; preparando presents the activity in progress.
Está matches Rosa; colocando stays unchanged.

lessons.title: Read Two Verbs as One Pattern
lessons.summary: Recognize starting, stopping, repeating, recent actions and obligation.
lessons.grammarTerm: Read Two Verbs as One Pattern
keywords: Recognize starting, stopping, repeating, recent actions and obligation.

examples.explanation: Dejar de changes the action into something that ceased.
Empezar a introduces the beginning.

lessons.title: Measure Time from the Right Moment
lessons.summary: Distinguish ongoing duration, a completed span and time ago.
lessons.grammarTerm: Measure Time from the Right Moment
keywords: Distinguish ongoing duration, a completed span and time ago.

examples.spanish: Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
examples.english: I have lived here for two years.
examples.explanation: The situation continues now; present vivo is natural.

examples.spanish: Vivía allí desde hacía ocho años.
examples.english: He/she had been living there for eight years.
examples.explanation: The duration is measured to a past reference point.

lessons.title: Follow Words Retold by Someone Else
lessons.summary: Track tense, person and reference when dialogue becomes narration.
lessons.grammarTerm: Follow Words Retold by Someone Else
keywords: Track tense, person and reference when dialogue becomes narration.

examples.spanish: Ana dijo que tenía la llave.
examples.english: Ana said she had the key.
examples.explanation: Tenía presents possession relative to Ana’s past statement.

examples.spanish: Le explicó que Clara había desaparecido.
examples.english: She explained to him that Clara had disappeared.
examples.explanation: The disappearance precedes the past explanation.

lessons.title: Recognize Wishes and Requests in the Past
lessons.summary: Understand regresara and explicara outside hypothetical if clauses.
lessons.grammarTerm: Recognize Wishes and Requests in the Past
keywords: Understand regresara and explicara outside hypothetical if clauses.

examples.spanish: Le pidió que explicara el sistema.
examples.english: He/she asked him/her to explain the system.
examples.explanation: The past request governs explicara.

examples.spanish: Esperó a que regresara la electricidad.
examples.english: He/she waited for the electricity to return.
examples.explanation: Regresara is part of what was awaited.

lessons.title: Wait Until It Happens
lessons.summary: Choose mood in time clauses by whether the event is anticipated or presented as factual.
keywords: Choose mood in time clauses by whether the event is anticipated or presented as factual.

examples.explanation: The indicative presents a habitual relationship.

examples.english: When he/she arrives, he/she will call.
examples.explanation: The arrival is anticipated from the current reference.

lessons.title: After a Preposition: Mí, Ti, Él
lessons.summary: Recognize the pronoun forms used after para, de and other prepositions.
lessons.grammarTerm: After a Preposition: Mí, Ti, Él
keywords: Recognize the pronoun forms used after para, de and other prepositions.

examples.spanish: Este lugar es especial para mí.
examples.english: This place is special to me.
examples.explanation: Para is followed by mí, not the subject form yo.
The preposition a introduces the pronoun él.

lessons.title: Follow the Thread of a Story
lessons.summary: Read sequence, continuation and contrast signals.
lessons.grammarTerm: Follow the Thread of a Story
keywords: Read sequence, continuation and contrast signals.

examples.english: At first they talked about the problem.
examples.explanation: Al principio marks an initial stage.

examples.english: He/she was still waiting for a reply.
examples.explanation: Todavía signals continuation.

lessons.title: When Se Does More Than Mean Self
lessons.summary: Read llamarse, irse and changes of state as whole verb patterns.
lessons.grammarTerm: When Se Does More Than Mean Self
keywords: Read llamarse, irse and changes of state as whole verb patterns.

examples.explanation: Llamarse is learned as a whole naming pattern.

examples.spanish: Clara se sentó en un banco.
examples.english: Clara sat down on a bench.
examples.explanation: Sentarse presents the act of sitting down.

lessons.title: Read Some, Every, Another, and None
lessons.summary: Track quantity and recover nouns that are left understood.
lessons.grammarTerm: Read Some, Every, Another, and None
keywords: Track quantity and recover nouns that are left understood.

examples.english: Every Thursday he/she prepares a table.
examples.explanation: Cada introduces a singular time unit.
Otra already expresses another; no una is needed.
